blocks.content: The story starts with a request that travels halfway around the world when it didn't have to.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274624334-428699653.png
blocks.alt: A request with no nearby region has to cross oceans and continents in both directions

blocks.content: A user in Mumbai opens your app. Your only server is in Virginia. The request crosses the Arabian Sea, the Middle East, Europe, the Atlantic, and lands in a data centre on the US East Coast. Then the response makes the same journey back. That round trip is roughly 200ms just for the network. Before your server does a single thing.
Now imagine you have servers in Mumbai, Singapore, Frankfurt, and Virginia. The right answer is obvious send the Mumbai user to Mumbai. But something has to make that decision.

Something has to look at an incoming request, understand where the user is, and route them to the right region. And then once they're in that region, something else has to distribute their request across the actual servers.
That's the distinction.

["A Global Load Balancer decides which region serves the user. 
","A Regional Load Balancer decides which server inside that region serves the request. 
"]
items: A Global Load Balancer decides which region serves the user.
A Regional Load Balancer decides which server inside that region serves the request.

blocks.content: They solve completely different problems, operate at completely different layers, and use completely different mechanisms.
1. Two Levels of Load Balancing
blocks.text: 1. Two Levels of Load Balancing

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785396520239-416822129.png
blocks.alt: Load balancing happens in two separate stages, which region and then which server

blocks.content: The diagram shows that load balancing is performed in two separate stages.

The first stage is the Global Load Balancer. When a user sends a request, the Global Load Balancer decides which region should handle that user. A user in India might be directed to the Mumbai region, a user in Europe to the Frankfurt region, and a user in the United States to the Virginia region. Its only responsibility is choosing the best region and directing the user there.

Once the user reaches the selected region, the Regional Load Balancer takes over. At this point, the region contains multiple servers capable of handling requests. The Regional Load Balancer decides which specific server inside that region should receive the traffic. It distributes requests across available servers so that no single server becomes overloaded.

The important idea is that these two load balancers perform different jobs. The Global Load Balancer decides which region should serve the user, while the Regional Load Balancer decides which server inside that region should handle the request.

Think of it like traveling to an office. First, you choose the correct city to visit. After reaching that city, you choose the specific building you need to enter. The Global Load Balancer chooses the city, and the Regional Load Balancer chooses the building.
2. Global Load Balancer
The global load balancer's job is geography. It answers one question: given this user's location, which of my regions should serve them?
It works through two mechanisms DNS-based routing and anycast. Understanding both is essential.
Mechanism 1: DNS-based global load balancing

When a user types yourapp.com, their browser makes a DNS query. Normally DNS just returns one IP address. With DNS-based global load balancing, the DNS server is smart it looks at where the DNS query came from and returns the IP address of the closest region.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274627656-325299910.png
blocks.alt: DNS-based global load balancing returns a different IP depending on where the query came from

blocks.content: The DNS TTL problemDNS responses are cached by client resolvers for the TTL duration (30s–5min). Failover is slow clients keep using the old IP until TTL expires.
Real examples of DNS-based global LB: AWS Route 53 with latency-based routing or geolocation routing. Cloudflare's nameservers. Akamai's global traffic management.
The DNS approach has one significant weakness: TTL caching. DNS responses are cached by resolvers and client OS caches for the TTL duration.
If you set TTL to 5 minutes and a region goes down, users who already cached the old IP will keep hitting the dead region for up to 5 minutes.
You can lower the TTL some services go as low as 30 seconds but very short TTLs increase DNS query load and some resolvers ignore them anyway.

blocks.content: Mechanism 2: Anycast routing

Anycast is a network-layer technique. You advertise the same IP address from multiple data centres simultaneously. The internet's routing infrastructure (BGP) naturally routes packets to the topographically nearest announcement of that IP.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274629323-953349587.png
blocks.alt: Anycast advertises the same IP everywhere and lets BGP naturally route to the nearest copy

blocks.content: Anycast has no TTL problem. When a PoP goes down, BGP reconverges within seconds and traffic automatically flows to the next nearest PoP.
This is why Cloudflare can absorb massive DDoS attacks without going down the attack traffic gets distributed across 300+ PoPs simultaneously, each absorbing a fraction.

The limitation: anycast works at Layer 3 (network). It routes packets to the nearest PoP but it doesn't understand HTTP, cookies, or user sessions. You can't do application-layer routing decisions with pure anycast. That's why Cloudflare pairs anycast with a reverse proxy at each PoP that handles the application layer.

blocks.content: 3. What the global LB decides
The global LB doesn't just route by geography. In a mature system it considers:

["Latency: route to the region with lowest measured round-trip time to this user. Not always the geographically closest (internet routing isn't a straight line).
","Health: if a region is down or degraded, don't route there. This is the most critical function during incidents.
","Capacity: if a region is at 95% capacity, stop sending new users there even if it's geographically closest. Route overflow to the next nearest region.
","Geofencing / compliance: European users must be served by European servers to comply with GDPR. Routing rules can enforce data residency.
","Traffic splitting: send 5% of traffic to a new region for canary testing before full rollout.
"]
items: Latency: route to the region with lowest measured round-trip time to this user. Not always the geographically closest (internet routing isn't a straight line).
Health: if a region is down or degraded, don't route there. This is the most critical function during incidents.
Capacity: if a region is at 95% capacity, stop sending new users there even if it's geographically closest. Route overflow to the next nearest region.
Geofencing / compliance: European users must be served by European servers to comply with GDPR. Routing rules can enforce data residency.
Traffic splitting: send 5% of traffic to a new region for canary testing before full rollout.

blocks.content: 4. Regional Load Balancer

Once a user arrives in a region, the regional load balancer takes over. This is a completely different problem. The user is already here now we need to pick which of the N servers inside this region handles their request.
Regional load balancers operate at two layers and which layer matters enormously.
1. Layer 4 (Transport) load balancing
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274630951-871233519.png
blocks.alt: A Layer 4 load balancer routes purely on packet headers, never opening the HTTP request itself

blocks.content: The LB looks at the TCP/UDP packet header source IP, destination IP, source port, destination port. It makes routing decisions based purely on this. It never reads the HTTP request inside.
This makes it extremely fast it can handle millions of connections per second because it's just shuffling IP packets.
2. Layer 7 (Application) load balancing
The LB reads the full HTTP request. This opens up a completely different class of routing decisions:

["/api/* → route to API server pool
","/images/* → route to static asset servers
","Cookie: user_tier=premium → route to premium server pool
","Content-Type: application/grpc → route to gRPC backends
","Authorization: Bearer  → validate auth before forwarding
"]
items: /api/* → route to API server pool
/images/* → route to static asset servers
Cookie: user_tier=premium → route to premium server pool
Content-Type: application/grpc → route to gRPC backends
Authorization: Bearer  → validate auth before forwarding

blocks.content: Layer 7 is what AWS ALB, nginx, Envoy, and Istio do. The cost is CPU reading and parsing HTTP adds overhead. But at regional scale, this overhead is entirely worth it for the routing intelligence you gain.

blocks.content: 5. Load balancing algorithms
The regional LB has N healthy backend servers. Which one gets the next request?

["Round Robin: Round Robin distributes requests to servers in a fixed sequence. The first request goes to Server 1, the second to Server 2, the third to Server 3, and then the cycle repeats. It is simple, easy to implement, and works well when all servers have similar capacity and the application is stateless.
","Least Connections: Least Connections sends each new request to the server currently handling the fewest active connections. This helps balance load more effectively when some requests take much longer to complete than others. It is commonly used in applications with varying request durations.
","IP Hash: IP Hash uses the client's IP address to determine which server should handle the request. This means the same client is usually routed to the same server every time, providing session affinity or sticky sessions. However, it can lead to uneven traffic distribution if some clients generate significantly more traffic than others.
","Weighted Round Robin: Weighted Round Robin is similar to Round Robin, but each server is assigned a weight based on its capacity. Servers with higher weights receive more requests than servers with lower weights. This is useful when some servers are more powerful than others or when gradually sending a small percentage of traffic to a new version during a canary deployment.
"]
items: Round Robin: Round Robin distributes requests to servers in a fixed sequence. The first request goes to Server 1, the second to Server 2, the third to Server 3, and then the cycle repeats. It is simple, easy to implement, and works well when all servers have similar capacity and the application is stateless.

Least Connections: Least Connections sends each new request to the server currently handling the fewest active connections. This helps balance load more effectively when some requests take much longer to complete than others. It is commonly used in applications with varying request durations.

IP Hash: IP Hash uses the client's IP address to determine which server should handle the request. This means the same client is usually routed to the same server every time, providing session affinity or sticky sessions. However, it can lead to uneven traffic distribution if some clients generate significantly more traffic than others.

Weighted Round Robin: Weighted Round Robin is similar to Round Robin, but each server is assigned a weight based on its capacity. Servers with higher weights receive more requests than servers with lower weights. This is useful when some servers are more powerful than others or when gradually sending a small percentage of traffic to a new version during a canary deployment.

blocks.content:
In practice: Round robin for stateless APIs. 

Least connections for anything with variable response times (file uploads, database-heavy queries). 

Weighted round robin for canary deployments new version gets 5% weight, old gets 95%, you gradually shift. 

IP hash is largely replaced by centralised session stores (Redis) sticky sessions via IP hash break when servers are added or removed.
blocks.title: Note

blocks.content: 6. Health checks
Every regional LB continuously health-checks its backend pool. If a server fails its health check, the LB stops routing to it instantly. No human intervention required.
Health checks range from simple to sophisticated:

["TCP check: can I open a TCP connection to port 8080? Cheapest. Doesn't tell you if the app is working, just if the port is open.
","HTTP check: does GET /health return 200? Much better. Your /health endpoint can verify database connectivity, cache connectivity, and any other dependency.
","Deep health check: does the health endpoint actually query the database, verify cache, check third-party APIs? Most expensive but most accurate. Catches \"the server is up but broken\" scenarios that simpler checks miss.
"]
items: TCP check: can I open a TCP connection to port 8080? Cheapest. Doesn't tell you if the app is working, just if the port is open.
HTTP check: does GET /health return 200? Much better. Your /health endpoint can verify database connectivity, cache connectivity, and any other dependency.

Deep health check: does the health endpoint actually query the database, verify cache, check third-party APIs? Most expensive but most accurate. Catches "the server is up but broken" scenarios that simpler checks miss.

blocks.content: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274632477-607810580.png
blocks.alt: A regional load balancer keeps healthy servers in the pool and removes the one that stops responding

blocks.content: The Regional Load Balancer continuously checks the health of all backend servers by sending requests to the /healthendpoint every few seconds.
In this example, Server 1 and Server 3 respond with 200 OK, so they are considered healthy and remain in the load balancing pool. New user requests can be sent to them.
Server 2 does not respond and times out, so the load balancer marks it as unhealthy and removes it from the pool. No new traffic is sent to that server until it becomes healthy again.
This process is called a health check, and it helps ensure that users are only routed to working servers.
7. The complete picture
How a user request travels through both the global and regional load balancers.
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274634188-36152280.png
blocks.alt: A single request passes through the global load balancer, then the regional load balancer, then one backend

blocks.content: When a user in Mumbai requests yourapp.com, the request first reaches the Global Load Balancer. Its job is to find the nearest healthy region. Since the Mumbai region is available, it routes the user there.

After the request reaches the Mumbai region, it is forwarded to the Regional Load Balancer. This load balancer manages all the backend servers inside that region. It distributes incoming traffic across healthy servers, handles TLS/HTTPS connections, and performs request routing.
In this example, Backend 1, Backend 2, and Backend 3 are all healthy. The Regional Load Balancer spreads traffic among them so that no single server becomes overloaded.
In simple terms:

["Global Load Balancer → Chooses the region
","Regional Load Balancer → Chooses the server inside that region
"]
items: Global Load Balancer → Chooses the region
Regional Load Balancer → Chooses the server inside that region

blocks.content: So the request flow is:

["User → Global Load Balancer → Mumbai Region → Regional Load Balancer → Backend Server.
"]
items: User → Global Load Balancer → Mumbai Region → Regional Load Balancer → Backend Server.

blocks.content: 8. Failover scenarios

Scenario 1: One Server Crashes: If one server in the Mumbai region crashes, the Regional Load Balancer quickly detects that the server is not responding. It removes that server from its list and sends traffic only to the remaining healthy servers. Users usually do not notice any problem because the Regional Load Balancer handles the failure automatically.

Scenario 2: Entire Mumbai Region Goes Down: If the whole Mumbai region becomes unavailable, the Global Load Balancer detects that the region is no longer responding. It stops sending new users to Mumbai and redirects them to another healthy region, such as Singapore. Existing users connected to Mumbai may need to reconnect, and their sessions could be lost unless session data is shared across regions.

DNS Cache Problem: Even after Mumbai is removed, some users may still have Mumbai's IP address stored in their DNS cache. They continue trying to connect to Mumbai until the cache expires. To reduce this delay, companies use very short DNS cache times or technologies like Anycast routing.

Scenario 3: Mumbai Is Healthy but Overloaded: Sometimes a region is working correctly but is handling too much traffic. In this case, the Global Load Balancer sends fewer new users to Mumbai and redirects more traffic to other regions such as Singapore or Frankfurt. This helps prevent overload and keeps response times fast.
9. Real-world tools
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274635787-472335686.png
blocks.alt: Global and regional load balancing are handled by genuinely different, purpose-built tools

blocks.content: 10. Side-by-side comparison
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/hld-content-images/1785274637287-981842225.png
blocks.alt: Global and regional load balancers differ in what they decide, how they decide it, and how fast they fail over

blocks.content: 11. HLD interview ( how to talk about this )
blocks.text: 11. HLD interview ( how to talk about this )

blocks.content: When you're designing a globally distributed system, bring both layers up explicitly. Interviewers want to see that you understand they solve different problems.
1. Start with the global layer.
Since we need to serve users across multiple continents, I'll put a global load balancer in front something like Cloudflare or AWS Route 53 with latency-based routing.
This routes each user to the nearest healthy region. If a whole region goes down, the global LB detects it via health checks and stops routing there users automatically go to the next nearest region.
2. Add the regional layer inside each region.
blocks.text: 2. Add the regional layer inside each region.

blocks.content: Within each region, we have a fleet of backend servers behind a regional load balancer an AWS ALB.

It handles TLS termination, distributes traffic with least-connections algorithm, does Layer 7 routing so /api goes to the API pool and /static goes to cache servers, and health-checks every backend every 10 seconds.
A server crash is detected in under 30 seconds and traffic is redistributed without any manual intervention.
3. Name the DNS TTL problem when relevant.
blocks.text: 3. Name the DNS TTL problem when relevant.

blocks.content: The main weakness of DNS-based global LB is that failover is bounded by the TTL clients cache the DNS response.

With a 60-second TTL, there's a 60-second window during regional failover where some users are still hitting the dead region. Anycast solves this by doing failover at BGP level, which reconverges in seconds.
4. Connect to stateful session handling.
One important consideration: if users have sessions tied to a specific region and that region fails, those sessions are lost.
We handle this by storing sessions in a globally replicated store like DynamoDB Global Tables or Redis with cross-region replication so any region can serve any user's session after failover.

The engineers who give the strongest answers are the ones who talk about failure modes not just the happy path. What happens when a server dies. What happens when a region dies. How long does failover take. What do users experience. That's what separates a textbook answer from a production-engineering answer.
